{"sample_id": "blind-99b0021429db45c1b4b8a0647c3b15f1", "theorem": "I have an \(n \times n\) sheet of stamps, from which I've been asked to tear out blocks of three adjacent stamps in a single row or column. (I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let \(b(n)\) be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that

\[
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
\]

for all \(n>0\).", "assumptions": [], "domain": "usamo", "explicit_subgoals": [], "candidate_text": "Let the cells be indexed by \((r,s)\), where \(1\le r,s\le n\). We may assume \(n\) is a positive integer.

For \(n\ge3\), there are
\[
2n(n-2)
\]
potential blocks of three consecutive cells: \(n(n-2)\) horizontal and the same number vertical. In a final configuration admitting no further block, every potential block contains a removed stamp.

A removed horizontal block meets at most five horizontal potential blocks: their starting columns can range over at most five values. Its three cells each lie in at most three vertical potential blocks, so it meets at most nine vertical potential blocks. Thus it meets at most fourteen potential blocks altogether. The same bound holds for a removed vertical block. Consequently,
\[
14b(n)\ge 2n(n-2),
\]
so
\[
b(n)\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
For \(n=1,2\), the same inequality holds because \(b(n)=0\). Hence we may take \(c=2/7\).

For the upper bound, consider the infinite periodic marking in which \((r,s)\) is marked exactly when
\[
s+2r\pmod 5\in\{0,1,2\}.
\]
In each fixed row, the marked cells occur in disjoint runs of three consecutive cells, separated by two unmarked cells. From the \(n\times n\) sheet, tear out every such marked run that lies wholly within the sheet. These are disjoint horizontal three-stamp blocks. There are at most \(n/5+1\) of them in each row, hence at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n
\]
in total.

The infinite marking meets every horizontal triple, since no row has three consecutive unmarked cells. It also meets every vertical triple: for three consecutive rows in a fixed column, the residues \(s+2r\) are
\[
a,\ a+2,\ a+4\pmod5,
\]
which are distinct, and therefore cannot all belong to the two unmarked residues \(\{3,4\}\).

Let \(E\) consist of the first two and last two columns of the sheet; thus \(|E|\le4n\). Every marked cell whose column lies between \(3\) and \(n-2\) belongs to a marked run lying wholly inside the sheet. It follows that after the preceding removals, every surviving potential block intersects \(E\).

Now continue greedily, tearing out any available three-stamp block until none remains. Removing stamps cannot create a new block, so every additionally removed block intersects \(E\). Since these additional blocks are disjoint, each uses a distinct stamp of \(E\); hence there are at most \(4n\) of them. We have therefore produced a maximal configuration using at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n+4n=\frac15n^2+5n
\]
blocks. Thus \(b(n)\le \frac15n^2+5n\), so one may take \(d=5\).

Therefore, for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
\frac17n^2- rac27n\le b(n)\le \frac15n^2+5n.
\]"}
